data.title: These 2 ‘Monster Growth’ Stocks Aren’t Done Climbing, Say Analysts
data.description:
Ask any old-school market investor and he’ll tell you that the cliché is true, and ‘past performance cannot guarantee future returns.’ If that were true without exception, then growth investing would not be a viable option – but we all know that investors love to buy into stocks that have shown enormous growth in recent months. The ‘monster growth’ stocks are popular because investing into them is successful.

The key is understanding the smart middle way, and treating stocks as individuals, with idiosyncratic features that need to be taken case by case. Past performance can be a solid indicator, even if it’s not a guarantee, and when it’s paired with consistent long-term gains, it’s a powerful indicator indeed.

You can double check that by checking in with the Wall Street analysts, the professional stock experts who’ve built careers and reputations on the quality of their published analyses. And right now, some of Wall Street’s pros are saying that the growth stocks are not done climbing.

Boil it down, and the factors to look for are strong gains, top ratings from the Street’s analysts, and a solid outlook for the future. Find a stock with all of those, and chances are, you’ve on to someting. We’ve opened up the TipRanks database to get the scoop on two stocks that match that profile. Here’s a closer look at them.

Adlai Nortye, Ltd. (ANL)

The first growth stock we’ll look at here is Adlai Nortye, a biopharmaceutical researcher working on a global stage. The company operates at the clinical-trial stage, and has several drug candidates undergoing investigation at various early-study levels. Adlai’s drug development research focuses on the creation of novel cancer therapies, based primarily on two therapeutic areas: precision RAS pathway targeted therapies, and next-gen PD-1/L1 pathway modulating immunotherapies.

The first of these therapeutic areas includes the drug candidates AN9025, an oral pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor, and AN4035, a CEACAM5-targeting ADC. Together, these new drug candidates are targeting various RAS-addicted tumors, a class of malignancies that includes a large proportion of all cancers, and is particularly well-represented in such dangerous conditions as pancreatic cancer, colorectal cancer, and certain lung cancers.

AN9025 is currently undergoing a global Phase I clinical trial, and dosed the first patient earlier this year. The trial focuses on patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors harboring RAS mutations. The first US patient in the once-daily dosing regimen was started in February, while the first US patient in the once-weekly regimen was started in July. In the first half of next year, the company expects to release initial data from the once-daily dosing segment of the study.

The second drug candidate to look at, AN4035, is a first-in-class RAS-inhibitor antibody drug conjugate (ADC) targeting CEACAM5, and it carries a highly potent pan-RAS(ON) inhibitor payload for therapeutic action. In July, the company received regulatory approval, from the Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC), in Australia for a Phase 1 clinical trial, and expects to follow up with an IND submission in the US. Patient dosing is expected to begin this year, with clinical data available during 2H27.

We should note that ANL saw its share price jump twice this year, in February and April, after two rounds of successful private-placement equity financing. Together, the two rounds raised $290 million, and the company reported having $231.9 million in liquid assets available as of June 30, 2026. This compared favorably to the $8.1 million available at the end of last year. For the year-to-date, shares in ANL have gained a truly impressive 957%.

This biotech stock has caught the attention of JonesTrading analyst Boris Peaker, a 5-star expert in the field. Peaker sees high potential in this company’s research track, with solid prospects of high revenues before the 2030s run out. He writes, “In our view, Adlai’s lead assets provide the company with two differentiated shots on goal for RAS-addicted malignancies, which constitute ~20% of all cancers and is particularly enriched in certain pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancer types. The company is lagging behind key competitors Revolution Medicines and Erasca, but has differentiated assets with potential for best-in-class efficacy and combinability. Currently, we are valuing ANL’s two lead assets (and not AN8025) in late-line, relapse/refractory PDAC, CRC, and NSCLC until we get further clarification on which indication/settings the company will pursue for initial regulatory approvals. However, with broad approval in these indications, we estimate WW peak revenue potential of ~$10B in 2038 with a weighted average POS/market penetration of 22%/27%.”

The prospect of a known timeline for profitability is an attractive feature for biopharma stocks, and Peaker rates ANL as a Buy, with a $22 price target that implies a one-year upside potential of 46.5%. (To watch Peaker’s track record, click here.)

Overall, ANL’s Strong Buy consensus rating, based on 4 recent reviews, is unanimous, showing that Wall Street likes what it sees here. The stock is trading for $15.01 and its $24.67 average target price is somewhat more bullish than Peaker allows, and suggests a gain of 64% on the one-year horizon. (See ANL stock forecast.)

data.title: Tesla Stock’s Cybercab Event Disappoints, and Shares Fall. This Analyst Sees Another 90% Drop
data.description:
Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) shares are falling in Friday’s session, representing a reversal of Thursday’s action. The stock gained more than 5% yesterday as investors looked ahead to the company’s latest step toward autonomous ride-hailing. The excitement was centered on the Cybercab event and Elon Musk’s ambition to challenge Waymo in the self-driving market.

By Friday, however, that enthusiasm had evaporated. TSLA shares are down 6.5% as of writing.

The company said Cybercab rides would open to the public in “limited areas” of Austin, Texas, at 5 p.m. CT on Friday. But the highly anticipated launch event itself was remarkably low-key. There was no livestream, journalists were excluded, and Elon Musk did not attend. Instead, Tesla invited a small group of largely pro-Tesla content creators, who were given rides in the two-seat vehicle.

Promotion

Explore TSLQ for 2X short leverage on TSLA

The company also provided few details about the commercial rollout. It did not disclose pricing or a specific deployment target, while Tesla’s app reportedly did not allow users to request a Cybercab ride as of Thursday night. There are 45 Cybercabs registered in Texas.

Adding to the disappointment, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an investigation into the Cybercab’s self-certification under federal vehicle safety standards, focusing on the vehicle’s lack of a steering wheel and conventional pedals. Questions also remain over potential resistance from states to Tesla’s camera-only approach to autonomous driving.

For GLJ Research analyst Gordon Johnson, the muted event was hardly surprising. “We’ve learned to keep a simple rule for Tesla product launches: count what can be counted. Last night we could count one thing, and that was 45 Cybercab registrations with the Texas DMV as of Wednesday,” Johnson said.

The analyst argues that Tesla failed to provide several of the metrics investors were looking for, including deployment targets, pricing and a consumer ordering option. “Attendees, a curated group of Tesla-friendly creators/cultists with instructions that plus-ones could not themselves be creators, took rides in a two-seater with no steering wheel and no pedals. Then they posted about it. That was the event,” he scathingly added.

Johnson does acknowledge that Tesla has made meaningful engineering progress, with the Cybercab going from little more than a stage prop in Burbank 23 months ago to carrying passengers on public roads today. “But the stock is not priced for a car,” he went on to say. “It is priced for a network, and on the network the company told us nothing it had not already said.”

Johnson also took aim at Wall Street’s expectations. Morgan Stanley had written ahead of the event that 25 to 50 Cybercabs operating across Texas could potentially lift Tesla shares, while the bullish scenario involved paid, unsupervised rides in Austin, Houston and Dallas.

Instead, Tesla delivered a much narrower rollout in Austin, with no clear indication of how many of the 45 registered vehicles are actually operating. “Sell-the-news” is Johnson’s conclusion, something investors apparently took to heart.

However, Johnson evidently thinks the stock is still completely overvalued. Along with a Sell rating, his $24.86 price target suggests the stock will fall another 93% over the next year. (To watch Johnson’s track record, click here)

Two other analysts are also TSLA bears, yet with an additional 11 Buys and 14 Holds, the stock claims a Moderate Buy consensus rating. At $377.08, the average price target suggests the stock will gain 7% in the months ahead. (See Tesla stock forecast)

data.title: Snowflake vs. Oracle: Bernstein Says One Enterprise AI Stock Is Undervalued, While the Other Faces Uncertainty
data.description:
Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) both sit at the heart of the enterprise data boom, but they are benefiting from it in different ways. Oracle has been turning its long-established database business into a much broader cloud and AI infrastructure operation, while Snowflake has built its business around helping companies make better use of the vast amounts of data they generate. That puts both companies in a position to benefit from the rapid adoption of AI, which is driving demand not only for computing power but also for the data infrastructure needed to train and run AI applications.

Their stocks, however, are telling very different stories right now. Oracle has spent much of the year under pressure (down by 20% year-to-date), with shares still well below last year’s record high as investors grapple with the enormous cost of its AI infrastructure ambitions.

Snowflake, by contrast, has also been under pressure earlier this year over fears AI will make software companies obsolete. But the company has just delivered a major earnings-fueled breakout, with shares surging more than 16% on Thursday after it beat Wall Street’s expectations and raised its full-year outlook, renewing investor confidence in its AI strategy.

Promotion

Bernstein analyst Mark Moerdler views the results as an impressive showing from the data warehouse company. Expectations were already elevated heading into the report, with investors looking for evidence of a meaningful pickup in revenue growth. Moerdler said Snowflake not only met those heightened expectations but delivered the additional catalyst needed to propel the stock higher.

The company’s product revenue growth accelerated to 37% from 34% in the prior quarter, coming in 4.5% ahead of consensus expectations. Snowflake also increased its FY27 product revenue growth forecast by five percentage points, taking it to 36% and pointing to a significant step-up in growth compared with last year.

According to management, the strength extended across the customer base rather than being concentrated in a particular group of clients. Moerdler noted that AI was an important contributor, while broader AI adoption was also creating tailwinds for Snowflake’s core business.

Snowflake is also seeing direct benefits from its AI offerings, particularly CoWork, previously known as Snowflake Intelligence, which enables data analysis and actions, and CoCo, formerly Cortex Codex, which is aimed at coding and development.

However, Moerdler sees a more difficult question emerging over the longer term. As important corporate data shifts into the cloud and SaaS providers and hyperscalers build out their own AI capabilities, it remains uncertain whether AI functionality will eventually move back into these core enterprise systems. While there is not enough evidence to answer that question yet, Moerdler said Snowflake’s progress to date has been impressive.

But that is not enough to support the bull case. “While we are encouraged by the innovation and execution focus under the new CEO, we remain concerned about longer-term competition with hyperscalers, AI labs and big SaaS vendors,” the 5-star analyst said. “At this valuation, we choose to stay on the sidelines.”

As such, Moerdler rates the stock as Market-Perform. Moerdler’s $377 price target implies shares will gain a modest 6% over the next year. (To watch Moerdler’s track record, click here)

Attention now turns to Oracle, which is set to release its fiscal first-quarter 2027 results next Thursday, Sept. 10. Moerdler said the stock remains an “extremely controversial and volatile” name, with the debate largely revolving around its push into AI datacenters. In particular, investors are concerned about the profitability and financial stability of the massive buildout, as well as Oracle’s ability to meet its significant cash needs and long-term contractual commitments.

However, Oracle’s revenue growth has been “steadily improving,” helped by Cloud revenue outpacing the company’s other businesses. That performance has been supported by OCI Gen II, including cloud database and AI, as well as Strategic Back Office offerings such as ERP and HCM.

Moerdler expects that momentum to carry into FY27, with the Cloud business serving as the primary engine of faster growth. In his view, Oracle’s current investment cycle could ultimately produce not only stronger revenue and earnings but also the technological capabilities and market credibility required to capture revenue from sovereign Cloud AI. “We believe that the company is nearing the end of its need for additional cash. The value being created is substantial and not included in the valuation,” the analyst commented.

To this end, Moerdler reiterated an Outperform (i.e., Buy) rating, backed by a $325 price target. Should the figure be met, investors will be pocketing returns of 111% one year from now.

Elsewhere on the Street, these stocks get plenty of support, with both claiming Strong Buy consensus ratings. With a $432.03 average price target, SNOW stock is expected to appreciate by 21% over the 12-month timeframe. ORCL shares are expected to climb by 65%, considering its average target lands at $254.68. (See SNOW stock forecast or ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: Why Lululemon Stock Is Getting Battered Today, and Why Morgan Stanley Sees More Pain Ahead
data.description:
Lululemon Athletica (NASDAQ:LULU) is having a rough end to the week. Shares are plunging in Friday’s session, down by 19% as of writing, after the athleisure company delivered another disappointing update, cutting its full-year sales outlook for the second time this year as weakness in China and growing competition in the U.S. continue to weigh on the business. The previous guidance reduction came in June, alongside the company’s first-quarter results.

The latest numbers suggest the recovery will take longer than investors had hoped. Lululemon now expects full-year sales of $10.35 billion to $10.50 billion, representing a 5% to 7% decline and a major reduction from its prior forecast of $11.0 billion to $11.50 billion. The $10.425 billion midpoint is also well below Wall Street’s forecast of $11.03 billion.

The earnings outlook has deteriorated just as sharply. Full-year adjusted earnings are now projected at $9.48 to $9.73 per share, compared with the previous forecast of $10.95 to $11.15 and analysts’ $10.93 estimate.

Straton views those changes as constructive, particularly the greater focus on brand-building, social media and community engagement. However, she expects incoming CEO Heidi O’Neill, who takes over on September 8, to make a “broader set of strategic adjustments.”

Straton estimates that a roughly 20% reduction to 2027 earnings could push consensus expectations toward $9 per share. That remains above her updated $8 forecast and the $6 estimate held by some of the more bearish analysts. “Thus,” says Straton, “we stay braced for negative EPS revisions & further valuation de-rating, keeping our Underweight (i.e., Sell) thesis intact.”

data.title: “It’s Outrageous,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) has become one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, as demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and other advanced memory products has surged. That has led to massive share price gains, allowing Micron to reach a market capitalization of more than $1 trillion, a milestone only a dozen or so other companies have attained. Yet despite the huge run-up, the company’s earnings have grown so quickly that its valuation remains surprisingly modest.

In fact, looking at its valuation, top investor James Foord, who ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, says the valuation is “absurd.”

At the current share price, Micron trades at roughly 22 times trailing earnings. But that multiple looks very different when compared with the company’s latest guidance. Using the midpoint of Micron’s fiscal fourth-quarter EPS guidance and annualizing it, the stock trades at less than eight times earnings. “At 20 P/E (at the time of Foord’s article), Micron already looks undervalued, and this becomes ridiculous once we annualize the coming quarter’s earnings, which will be confirmed in less than a month,” says the 5-star investor. “Micron trades at just over 7x those annualized earnings, and that tells me that the market does not believe this can continue.”

Promotion

This is where Nvidia enters the picture. When Nvidia reported its fiscal second-quarter 2027 results, it said that its supply commitments had more than doubled in a single quarter, from $119 billion to $279 billion. That increase was mostly linked to memory procurement, providing evidence that demand and pricing power remain exceptionally strong.

However, Nvidia is also looking for ways to use less HBM. Its Rubin CPX accelerator uses cheaper GDDR7 memory for certain workloads, while Nvidia has also paid $20 billion to license Groq’s architecture, which relies heavily on extremely fast SRAM built directly into the processor.

That matters because HBM is one of the most profitable parts of the memory market. If Nvidia can move some of the most bandwidth-intensive AI workloads onto alternative memory architectures, HBM pricing could eventually come under pressure, hurting Micron’s margins.

Foord nevertheless believes the threat should not be overstated. SRAM currently has nowhere near enough capacity to replace HBM for the enormous AI models being developed today. The fastest workloads may run on SRAM, but the rest still needs to reside in HBM or conventional DRAM.

There is another important point: Micron is a memory manufacturer, not simply an HBM company. If AI systems shift some demand from HBM toward GDDR7 or standard DRAM, that could change Micron’s product mix rather than eliminate the underlying memory demand.

Foord will therefore be watching how much HBM Nvidia puts into its next-generation systems, whether Micron can maintain premium pricing for customized HBM4E, and how its roughly $100 billion of long-term customer agreements are renewed.

For now, the investor remains bullish. Micron’s FQ4 guide suggests “another record quarter,” and while the architectural shift could pressure HBM margins, Foord does not believe it signals the end of the AI memory boom. Nvidia’s $279 billion in supply commitments suggest the industry still expects to need enormous amounts of memory.

To this end, Foord rates MU stock a Buy. (To watch Foord’s track record, click here)

Barring one Street analyst who remains on the sidelines, all 30 other recent reviews are positive, making the consensus view a Strong Buy. At $1,554.67, the average price target points toward 12-month gains of 58%. (See Micron stock forecast)

data.title: Marvell or Broadcom: Buy the Dip in Only One AI Stock, Says Top RBC Analyst
data.description:
Marvell (NASDAQ:MRVL) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) are two major players in the semiconductor industry and key rivals in the race to supply the custom chips and networking technology powering AI data centers.

Broadcom remains the much larger of the two, with a market value of roughly $1.8 trillion versus around $180 billion for Marvell, and it has a substantially broader business spanning semiconductors and infrastructure software. Marvell is a more focused semiconductor company, but it has been gaining ground in custom AI silicon and going head-to-head with Broadcom for business from the hyperscalers building their own AI chips.

Both also disappointed investors with their latest quarterly readouts. The headline numbers came in ahead of Wall Street’s estimates, but they still fell short of the sky-high expectations investors had set.

Its third-quarter outlook of $3.15 billion in revenue and $1.10 in EPS also topped the analyst’s estimates of $3.0 billion and $1.05 and consensus of $3.0 billion and $1.08.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast from $11.5 billion to $12.0 billion and its fiscal 2028 outlook from $16.5 billion to $18.0 billion, implying annual growth of 45% and 50%, respectively, compared with previous expectations of 40% and 45%.

The strength was broad-based, with Marvell’s optical business benefiting from robust demand for 800G and 1.6T products and growing adoption of scale-up architectures.

Meanwhile, management expects its custom business to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027 and more than double in fiscal 2028, driven by progress with AWS Trainium and Microsoft’s MAIA XPU program. It also expects “significant acceleration” in fiscal 2029. XPU-attach programs, particularly CXL and memory expansion, are seeing strong adoption among hyperscalers as inference workloads drive demand and memory remains scarce.

Marvell provided limited details on its recently announced Google agreement, with more information expected at its October 6 analyst day. However, management reiterated its projection for more than $10 billion in custom revenue in fiscal 2029 and indicated a “significant upside bias” to previous estimates. The lack of detail might have upset investors somewhat but is not a big deal to Pajjuri. “We are not overly concerned and fully expect Google program ramps to inflect in FY29, which should drive sizable upside to current $10B+ custom revenue target,” the 5-star analyst said. “We raise estimates and believe premium valuation is justified given 45%+ topline growth, optical connectivity leadership, and strong custom XPU pipeline.”

Accordingly, Pajjuri raised his fiscal 2027 EPS estimate from $4.02 to $4.19 and his fiscal 2028 estimate from $6.01 to $6.51. He maintained an Outperform rating on the stock along with a $360 price target, a figure pointing toward 12-month returns of 72%. (To watch Pajjuri’s track record, click here)

Turning to Broadcom, its fiscal third-quarter results were also ahead of expectations, with revenue of $29.6 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $3.32, compared with the analyst’s estimates of $29.4 billion and $3.22 and the Street’s estimates of $29.2 billion and $3.22. AI revenue surged 221% year over year to $16.7 billion, exceeding the company’s previous guidance of $16 billion, while a 75% gross margin was about 150 basis points above consensus despite a higher XPU mix.

Broadcom’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue forecast of $34.8 billion was broadly in line with consensus of $34.7 billion, while its $21.7 billion AI revenue forecast was slightly above the analyst’s roughly $21 billion estimate.

The company raised its fiscal 2027 AI revenue forecast to $115 billion from more than $100 billion, generally matching Pajjuri’s expectations but falling short of consensus at $123 billion. Management also pointed to strong demand from its six XPU customers and introduced a fiscal 2028 AI revenue forecast of $230 billion, driven mostly by its engagements with Anthropic and OpenAI.

Pajjuri said the extended visibility was encouraging but highlighted component supply and infrastructure readiness as “potential limiting factors.” He also noted that LLM companies have supply and financing agreements with multiple chip suppliers and cloud-service providers, creating uncertainty around silicon allocation. At roughly 18.5 times estimated 2027 earnings, Broadcom is trading at a premium of more than 30% to Nvidia on a stock-compensation-adjusted basis. “We see balanced risk/reward as solid customer engagements and multi-year visibility are outweighed by supply/LPS limitations and what we consider is a high bar for FY27/28,” he summed up.

To this end, Pajjuri rates AVGO as Sector Perform (i.e., Neutral). His $400 price target suggests shares will gain 12% over the next year.

data.title: Insiders Are Buying These 2 Stocks — Should You Take the Hint?
data.description:
There’s only one real trick to stock investing, but it’s a doozy. You have to figure out the right stocks to build your portfolio. There are thousands of them out there, and thousands of traders dealing in them, and their tens of millions of transactions make for a lot of noise. You need to find a signal that will cut through all of that.

This is where the insiders can make a difference for the outsiders. ‘Insider’ might sound nefarious, but it’s not – it’s just the corporate officers and board members, the senior execs whose positions make them front-row observers to company operations and opportunities and challenges. The insiders know the business, know its ins and outs, and they’ll use that knowledge when they decide to invest their own money.

Of course, you have to be aware of an important feature when insiders buy or sell their own companies’ shares. They’ll have lots of reasons to sell, from diversifying their holdings to covering taxes to liquidating for capital – but they’ll typically only have one reason to buy: they believe the shares will appreciate in value, and soon.

Dick’s Sporting Goods (DKS)

The first stock we’ll look at here, Dick’s, holds the distinction of being the US market’s largest multi-channel sporting goods retailer. The company is the dominant player in this field, offering customers varied lines of athletic equipment, apparel, footwear, and outdoor gear, including such items as high-end workout shoes, camping gear, outdoor clothing, firearms – and, of course, fishing gear and tackle, which is how the chain got its start in 1948.

Today, Dick’s is a $12 billion giant. In its fiscal year 2025, which ended on January 31, 2026, Dick’s brought in over $17 billion in total revenue. That was up some 28% year-over-year, an increase driven by the company’s acquisition of the athletic shoe retailer Foot Locker in September of 2025. The Foot Locker move gave Dick’s a much stronger position in athletic footwear, adding a major sneaker-focused retail business to its existing sporting-goods operations.

We should note here that DKS shares dropped sharply at the end of August, after the company missed badly against the expectations on its fiscal 2Q26 results. The company reported a top line of $5.59 billion, for a year-over-year gain of more than 53%, and reported a non-GAAP EPS of $3.53. But the EPS was down year-over-year from $4.38, and it missed the forecast by 23 cents per share. Revenue missed by $56.6 million. The stock fell more than 30% in the aftermath of the earnings release, and is down 36% for the past year.

That set the scene for the insider buys, with multiple purchases coming right after the drop in stock price at the end of August. Board members William Colombo, Robert Eddy, and Sandeep Mathrani all bought blocks ranging from 1,550 shares to 6,100. Mathrani laid out nearly $200K, while Eddy and Colombo paid $514K and $785.5K for their purchases. The big buy, however, came from Mark Barrenechea, also of the Board of Directors, who paid $2.222 million for 17,000 shares of DKS. Barrenechea now holds $3.82 million worth of the company’s stock.

Despite the headwinds with the Foot Locker segment, Bank of America analyst Lorraine Hutchinson believes that DKS shares will rebound going forward. She says of the company and its prospects, “We are encouraged by the strength of the Dick’s business in the face of these industry challenges, and expect 2H to represent a floor for fundamental performance at FL. With the stock now trading at 10x P/E and estimates rebased, we think continued strength at Dick’s will drive multiple expansion… The Dick’s business delivered a 4.9% comp, with core business growth even excluding the World Cup benefit. Strength remained broad-based across footwear, apparel, and hardlines, with strong trends in team sports, licensed product, running, cleats, outdoor, and emerging brands.”

Unsurprisingly, Hutchinson comes down with the bulls on Dick’s, rating the stock as a Buy, with a $200 price target that suggests a one-year upside potential of 43%. (To watch Hutchinson’s track record, click here.)

The event is expected to showcase the production version of Tesla’s purpose-built autonomous vehicle, a two-seat model without a steering wheel or pedals that the company plans to use in its expanding robotaxi network.

The launch is an important moment for Tesla’s autonomous-driving ambitions, but an investor with the moniker of Deep Value Investing (DVI), who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, is not convinced it will be the game-changer some investors expect.

The investor remains cautious about the company’s robotaxi strategy and believes there are several reasons to question how quickly the business can become a meaningful financial contributor.

A major concern is the gap between Tesla and Waymo when it comes to real-world autonomous driving experience. Waymo has now accumulated more than 200 million fully autonomous miles on public roads, compared with the roughly 380,000 miles of unsupervised robotaxi driving Tesla reported on its latest earnings call. DVI acknowledges that Tesla’s camera-based approach appears to have improved and does not dismiss the technology outright. However, the sheer difference in autonomous mileage highlights how much further Waymo has progressed.

Waymo is also completing more than 500,000 rides per week and has operations across roughly 11 U.S. markets. Tesla, meanwhile, has not disclosed a comparable weekly ride figure, making it difficult to measure the scale of its robotaxi operation. DVI therefore wants Tesla to provide clearer numbers at the Cybercab event, particularly on weekly rides and autonomous miles.

The Cybercab itself could give Tesla an advantage on costs. Tesla previously suggested the vehicle could cost less than $30,000 when produced at scale, while Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have historically been considerably more expensive. Its newer Ojai robotaxi appears cheaper than its Jaguar-based fleet but could still cost more than a Cybercab after hardware and import tariffs are included.

That lower cost is an important potential advantage, but the 5-star investor argues that execution remains the bigger question. Tesla’s automotive margins have deteriorated substantially from their 2021 levels, while its Services and Other segment generated a 14% gross margin in Q2. Robotaxi economics are not reported separately, so there is not yet enough evidence to show that the business is improving Tesla’s profitability.

data.title: Billionaire Dan Loeb Said Nvidia Stock Was Undervalued. Then He Sold All His Shares. Should You Do the Same?
data.description:
Dan Loeb is one of Wall Street’s best-known activist investors. He founded Third Point in 1995 and built the firm around concentrated, event-driven investments, often taking positions in companies where he believes there is an opportunity to unlock value.

That makes his latest move involving Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) particularly interesting.

Third Point completely exited its Nvidia position during the second quarter, selling its remaining 190,000 shares. But this was actually the final stage of a much larger sell-off. At the end of 2025, Third Point owned around 2.95 million Nvidia shares. It sold roughly 2.76 million of them during Q1, leaving just 190,000 shares, before selling the remainder in Q2.

Promotion

200% short exposure to NVDA with NVDS

What makes the sale even more interesting are recent comments the billionaire made. In June, Loeb said he believed Nvidia was still undervalued despite the company’s massive $5 trillion market cap.

So why did Loeb sell? One possible explanation is profit-taking. Third Point is not necessarily a buy-and-forget investor. Loeb tends to move money around when he sees better opportunities, and the average stock among the fund’s 20 largest positions had been held for just nine months as of June 30.

That makes the Nvidia sale look less like a straightforward bet against AI and more like a decision to take money off the table and redeploy it elsewhere. Loeb also sold Broadcom and Meta at the same time as Nvidia, while dramatically increasing his Alphabet position and opening a large new position in Warner Bros. Discovery. So it could be that Nvidia had performed well, but Loeb believes he can earn better returns elsewhere.

There is, however, definitely a case to ignore Loeb’s decision. Nvidia’s latest results were exceptionally strong. Fiscal second-quarter revenue jumped 56% sequentially and 73% year-over-year to $96.2 billion, while data-center revenue reached $89 billion. Adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share vs. Wall Street’s $2.09 estimate.

Importantly, Nvidia expects revenue of about $108 billion in the current quarter. Analysts had been expecting roughly $104.2 billion. The company is also forecasting around 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, far above Wall Street’s previous expectations of roughly 44%.

The company remains at the center of the AI infrastructure boom, and demand for its processors continues to exceed what it can supply. Its results suggest that the huge amounts being spent on AI infrastructure are still translating into enormous revenue growth.

There are some risks to the bull case, however. Higher memory costs could put pressure on Nvidia’s margins. Its business in China remains uncertain. And the biggest technology companies are developing their own AI chips, which could eventually reduce their reliance on Nvidia.

In any case, the Street’s analysts all disagree with Loeb’s move. The stock claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, based on a unanimous 30 Buys. At $329.32, the average price target implies shares will gain 45% over the one-year time frame. (See Nvidia stock forecast)

data.title: AMD vs. Oracle: One AI Stock Is a Buy, the Other’s Future Is Cloudy, Says Top Investor
data.description:
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) are both participating in the AI infrastructure boom but they play different roles. AMD supplies the CPUs and AI accelerators powering data centers and is taking on Nvidia in the market for AI chips. Its Helios rack-scale systems are designed to capture more of the accelerator opportunity. Oracle sits further down the chain, providing the cloud and data-center infrastructure needed to deploy AI computing at scale.

That gives both stocks exposure to the same powerful spending trend, but through very different business models. AMD must turn soaring accelerator demand into profitable growth while protecting margins, whereas Oracle is spending enormous sums to build the infrastructure required to fulfill its AI contracts.

Top investor Louis Gerard has been taking a closer look at both names and his analysis centers on whether those economics justify the current valuations.

Promotion

200% short exposure to ORCL with ORCZ

Assessing AMD, the chip giant’s latest results were strong. In Q2, revenue rose 50% year-over-year to $11.54 billion, while non-GAAP EPS jumped 82% to $1.66. Data center operating income swung from a loss a year earlier to $2.1 billion. AMD expects Q3 revenue of $12.7 billion to $13.3 billion, implying about 41% YoY growth and topping the $12.5 billion consensus estimate.

The main concern for Gerard is margins. AMD guided for 56% gross margin again despite expecting revenue to rise another 13% sequentially. Gerard sees HBM4 pricing as the key issue. AMD’s MI455X uses 432GB of HBM4, giving it a capacity advantage but also exposing it to higher memory costs. If HBM4 prices rise sharply into 2027, AMD could need roughly a 9%-10% increase in rack pricing simply to maintain current margins.

The 5-star investor believes that is manageable because Nvidia is also expected to raise server prices, indicating that higher memory costs can be passed on to hyperscalers. Demand remains strong, with the Helios rack-scale AI system entering production and accelerator demand reportedly running ahead of expectations. The bigger issue is valuation: AMD trades at more than 80 times non-GAAP earnings and has a free-cash-flow yield of only about 1.1%. Yet Gerard argues that AMD looks more attractive when viewed against forward earnings, with its valuation premium to Nvidia narrowing from roughly 2x to about 1.5x.

Despite the concerns, Gerard fancies AMD’s prospects, and therefore rates the stock a Buy. (To watch Gerard’s track record, click here)

Oracle presents a different set of challenges. At the end of FQ4 (May quarter), its RPO (remaining performance obligations) reached $638 billion, up 363% YoY, but fulfilling that backlog requires enormous investment. Oracle generated negative $23.7 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2026 and spent $55.7 billion on CapEx. Debt has climbed to roughly $167 billion, alongside substantial long-term data-center lease commitments.

One positive development is that many new AI infrastructure contracts are prepaid or involve customers supplying their own hardware. This shifts some capital risk away from Oracle and improves the returns on the capital it does deploy. However, Gerard notes that customer-supplied hardware also means Oracle captures less revenue and profit per gigawatt.

Ahead of Oracle’s September 10 earnings report, Gerard is focused on what the enormous backlog actually produces. He wants evidence on AI infrastructure margins, the number of gigawatts delivered, whether the $70 billion CapEx plan remains realistic, the makeup of the RPO and the company’s free cash flow and financing needs. Any indication that Oracle needs to raise more debt would be a particularly bearish signal.

Oracle looks cheap at around 20 times non-GAAP earnings, but Gerard argues that the multiple needs context. Those earnings are being generated while the company remains dependent on external financing and continues to spend heavily on infrastructure. Meanwhile, Amazon (AWS), Microsoft (Azure) and Google have stronger balance sheets and can compete aggressively in AI computing.

Oracle’s relatively cheap valuation and shift toward prepaid and customer-supplied contracts have improved its risk profile, but how profitable its massive AI infrastructure buildout will ultimately be remains unclear.

As such, Gerard maintains a Hold rating on the stock.

The Street’s analysts see no reason to pick between the pair, rating both as Strong Buys. AMD’s $647.19 average price target offers one-year upside of 45%. ORCL shares are expected to appreciate by 69%, given the average target clocks in at $254.57. (See AMD stock forecast or ORCL stock forecast)

data.title: Nvidia vs. Micron: Own One AI Stock, but Stay Away From the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) have both made the most of the AI opportunity, although they have benefited from it in different ways.

Nvidia has emerged as the dominant supplier of the GPUs and networking technology needed to power AI data centers, with hyperscalers and other customers spending heavily on its latest-generation chips. Micron, meanwhile, has benefited from the surge in demand for high-performance memory, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is essential for feeding AI accelerators with data. As AI models become more sophisticated and data center workloads grow, both companies are seeing their technologies become ever more critical to the AI infrastructure buildout.

NVDA’s share gains have catapulted it to the status as the world’s most valuable company, while more recently, Micron stock has delivered massive returns that have helped it join the $1 trillion+ market cap club.

Promotion

Learn why XOVR invested in Kalshi and the investment thesis behind one of its newest private holdings.

But which has better prospects moving forward? Investor Bruno Montoya Amador has been taking a look at both and thinks only one is worthy of investors’ cash right now.

Looking at chip king Nvidia, the company has continued to benefit from massive spending by hyperscalers and AI-focused cloud providers, with its latest results showing little sign of a slowdown. In Q2 FY27, revenue, gross profit, operating income, and net income climbed 106%, 113%, 124%, and 126%, respectively, compared to the year-ago period. AI infrastructure spending is also expected to reach roughly $800 billion in 2026, providing a powerful catalyst for Nvidia’s business.

The main concern is how long hyperscalers can sustain such enormous capital expenditures. Companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are developing their own AI chips, partly to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and its CUDA ecosystem. Montoya Amador sees this as a longer-term threat, particularly if custom-chip development becomes cheaper and more accessible. For now, though, Nvidia remains difficult to displace. Revenue from its hyperscale customers rose 102% YoY to $48.7 billion, while its AI cloud, industrial and enterprise business also grew rapidly.

Nvidia’s growing relationship with so-called NeoCloud providers is another area worth watching. The company has helped these businesses secure financing by committing to purchase computing capacity through take-or-pay agreements, essentially providing lenders with greater confidence in future cash flows. Montoya Amador believes the arrangement creates some risk because Nvidia can simultaneously act as an investor, seller, guarantor, and potential buyer of last resort. Still, he does not consider its $56 billion in disclosed commitments particularly alarming relative to Nvidia’s roughly $300 billion in trailing-12-month revenue. For him, the bigger issues are whether hyperscaler spending remains strong and whether those investments continue generating acceptable returns.

Overall, he rates Nvidia a Buy, while emphasizing the importance of monitoring hyperscaler capital spending, returns on investment and the growth of Nvidia’s commitments. (To watch Montoya Amador’s track record, click here)

Micron presents a different picture. The company delivered extraordinary fiscal Q3 2026 results, with revenue soaring 346% YoY and net income jumping nearly 1,400%. Yet the stock remains relatively inexpensive compared with many semiconductor peers, reflecting investors’ concerns about the highly cyclical nature of the memory market.

Micron is trying to reduce that cyclicality through new five-year SCAs (strategic customer agreements). Sixteen agreements cover roughly 20% of its DRAM volume and one-third of its NAND volume through 2030, with the company expecting about half or more of its revenue eventually to fall under these arrangements. The contracts include take-or-pay provisions and roughly $100 billion of minimum committed revenue from 14 agreements, providing Micron with much greater visibility than it historically enjoyed.

However, Montoya Amador remains skeptical. The key uncertainty is how much of these commitments actually relates to high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, the product at the heart of Micron’s AI-driven growth. Management’s wording that the agreements include “HBM as appropriate” leaves him unconvinced that a substantial portion of the commitments covers HBM. If the contracts mainly cover more commoditized DRAM and NAND, they may not protect Micron from a future decline in HBM pricing.

There is also the question of enforcement. Semiconductor companies have historically been reluctant to force customers to honor unfavorable long-term commitments when prices fall, because doing so can damage valuable customer relationships. For Montoya Amador, the contracts are promising but still too opaque to eliminate the fundamental risks of the memory cycle.

As a result, he rates Micron a Sell.

The Street agrees with only 50% of that thesis. Both stocks are rated as Strong Buys and are projected to deliver robust returns. Nvidia’s average price target lands at $329.32, suggesting the stock will gain 47% over the next year. Micron’s $1,556.55 average target offers 12-month upside of 63%. data.title: Wall Street vs. Short Sellers: 2 ‘Strong Buy’ Stocks That Could Squeeze
data.description:
Stock investing is all about balancing risk and reward, and nowhere is that more true than in short selling. Essentially, a short seller is betting that a stock will drop in price in the near-term; he sells ‘borrowed’ shares, hoping to close his position by buying them back, to return, at a lower price than he sold – and making a profit on the difference.

The conventional wisdom on short selling is that it’s an indication of clear weakness in a stock. After all, large-scale short-selling is a literal bet that the shares will lose money. But the facts on the ground are more complex, because high-value, fundamentally sound stocks can attract short sellers. In these cases, the short sellers are not actually betting against the stock, but they are betting that the share price will correct in the near-term.

Of course, the stock could gain – and that could trigger a short squeeze. It’s a classic trap. The short seller is betting on a near-term price drop, so he can eventually buy back the shares at a lower price, close his position, and turn a profit. But if the stock gains instead, he faces mounting losses – and could be forced to close his position at a loss.

Right now, Wall Street’s analysts and the risk-tolerant short sellers are at odds on two of the market’s ‘Strong Buy’ stocks. These are shares that have attracted significant short-selling interest in recent weeks – but the upside potential is still robust, and the Street’s analysts are still predicting good things. Will the short sellers get squeezed? We don’t know – but let’s take a closer look at both stocks and see what the analysts and the data are saying.

SoundHound AI, Inc. (SOUN)

We’ll start with SoundHound, a fascinating AI company that has brought AI tech into the realm of computerized voice and voice recognition applications. It’s a niche – but it’s a growing niche. Voice apps are popular for their easy interface and their hands-off nature, making them amenable to use in ‘distracted’ situations, such as while driving a car. SoundHound has prioritized natural speech in its AI-powered voice interface systems.

SoundHound delivers end-to-end conversational experiences across a wide range of channels, digital and physical, in kiosks or online chats, on smart devices or over smart TVs. The company uses AI to provide a natural conversation, which you may have experienced in drive-thrus, in cars, or over voice mail.

The company is actively working to improve its technology, to keep it at the forefront of the AI interface field. SoundHound’s OASYS platform is an agentic AI platform capable of self-learning and of orchestrating AI systems for enterprise clients. OASYS deploys AI agents that can handle a wide range of actions, including transactions, tasks, and workflows, to make life easier for end users, whether those are employees or customers.

In addition to improving its technology, through the OASYS platform, SoundHound is also looking to expand and improve its product lines and capabilities. In April of this year, the company entered into an agreement to acquire the customer-contact company LivePerson, in a move that will combine the leading voice-centered agentic AI with the leading digital-messaging chatbot provider. The transaction implies a total enterprise value of $250 million for the combined entity, and SoundHound is set to acquire LivePerson for an estimated equity value of $43 million. The transaction is expected to close on September 4.

Shares in SOUN have been volatile this year, and the stock is down 32% for the year-to-date. Looking at the short interest in the shares, according to the latest data (Aug 14), we see that roughly 40% of SoundHound’s float is sold short. That’s a tremendous percentage, and puts SoundHound among the most short-sold stocks on Wall Street right now.

On a positive note, SoundHound reported solid numbers in its 2Q26 earnings release. Revenue was an all-time high, at $61.9 million. This figure was up 45% year-over-year and beat the forecast by $9.5 million. At the bottom line, SoundHound is still operating at a net loss. In Q2, the non-GAAP net loss was listed as ($9.0) million; per share, this came to ($0.02), although it beat expectations by 3 cents per share.

For Cantor analyst Thomas Blakey, who covers this tech leader, the company’s technological precocity is the natural starting point. He writes, “These technological improvements (OASYS, internal LLMs) are improving win, renewal, and expansion rates and are key in terms of driving value creation in SoundHound AI’s M&A strategy centered on growing the installed base of recently acquired companies, which the company aims to do with LivePerson… SoundHound’s Voice Commerce (Pillar 3) appears on track, if not ahead of expectations, targeting launches with QSR customers and a potential new auto customer by end of year and now additively launching voice commerce in 2HC26 with a TV manufacturer.”

For Blakey, this combination of improving tech, intelligent M&A, and high expansion potential adds up to an Overweight (Buy) rating, along with a $15 price target that suggests a one-year upside potential of a hefty 121%. (To watch Blakey’s track record, click here.)

Those are solid results, so why is the stock falling so sharply?

Meanwhile, GAAP operating expenses more than doubled YoY, reaching $188.4 million vs. last year’s $89.6 million.

The company also expects FQ2 GAAP gross margin to come in between 62.9% and 64.9%. At the midpoint of 63.9%, that would represent another decline from the 64.5% reported in the first quarter.

So, the stock is taking a beating in today’s session, but the results haven’t altered Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg’s bullish thesis.

Svanberg notes that over the past year, Credo has transformed its business in a meaningful way. What was once a niche company focused on defining and supplying the active electrical cable (AEC) market has evolved into a more diversified connectivity provider. Its portfolio now includes both systems-level products and discrete components covering optical and copper connectivity, along with connectivity protocols such as Ethernet, PCIe, and UALink. The broader diversification is important because Credo is expanding its revenue base across different platforms and customers. At the same time, the company continues to spend heavily on R&D (research and development).

That has led investors to question whether AECs can continue powering the company’s unusually strong growth and financial performance. There are also questions about whether optical connectivity and Credo’s other products can eventually become large enough growth drivers to justify the stock’s valuation.

However, Svanberg sees the current valuation as particularly compelling when Credo is compared with other fast-growing AI data center companies in his coverage, including ALAB, MRVL, SMTC, and MTSI.

Based on Svanberg’s CY27E EPS estimates, Credo currently trades at the lowest P/E multiple (39.4x) among that group (Svanberg’s comparison uses share prices from the September 1 close, before the stock’s subsequent decline). Svanberg also included established analog semiconductor names ADI and TXN to highlight that Credo is now trading at valuations closer to companies with significantly slower growth.

However, the rally has lost some momentum in recent months. Despite its huge year-to-date gain, the stock is now more than 34% below the record high it reached at the end of June.

That sharp decline leaves investors with an important question: has the memory-chip stock finally run too far, or has the recent weakness created an attractive entry point? Keithen Drury, a top-rated investor who contributes to The Motley Fool, believes it is the latter. “I think now could be the perfect time to buy Sandisk stock, as the trends that pushed it higher at the start of the year are still prevalent,” the 5-star investor said. “These conditions will stick around for a while, and could be exactly what is needed to propel Sandisk to new highs before the year is over.”

The central argument comes down to a continuing shortage of NAND memory. Sandisk specializes in NAND, a type of memory used for long-term data storage in products including flash drives and solid-state drives (SSDs). Demand from data centers has surged, absorbing much of the available NAND supply and pushing prices significantly higher.

data.title: ‘It’s Years Away,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock has come under pressure as enthusiasm for AI stocks has waned recently. Concerns about competition and the traditionally cyclical nature of the memory-chip industry have impacted sentiment, while higher bond yields and interest rates have also weighed on tech and semiconductor stocks. Investors are also becoming more cautious about the enormous sums being spent on AI infrastructure and whether the eventual returns will justify the investment. As a result, Micron shares now sit about 23% below their June highs.

Nevertheless, despite the pullback, top investor Yiannis Zourmpanos believes Micron remains an attractive way to play the AI infrastructure boom. Zourmpanos, who ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, argues that the market may be underestimating how long the current memory shortage will last. High-bandwidth memory (HBM), which is essential for AI systems, is absorbing valuable DRAM production capacity, helping suppliers maintain unusually strong pricing power. SK hynix has even warned that memory shortages could persist as far out as 2030.

Zourmpanos points to recent memory pricing as evidence that the shortage is genuine rather than simply the result of customers stockpiling inventory. Server DRAM prices continue to rise as manufacturers allocate limited capacity toward HBM and other high-value products. Prices for 32GB DDR5 RDIMM spot modules recently reached around $1,665, having increased another 4.1% in a single week. PC manufacturers are also building inventories ahead of anticipated supply cuts, while suppliers are securing higher prices for future HBM products.

The investor also sees support for his argument from SK hynix, one of Micron’s largest competitors. Although SK hynix is investing billions of dollars in new production facilities, Zourmpanos argues that this does not necessarily mean an oversupply is imminent. Much of the spending is going toward constructing facilities that will not contribute significant additional memory production for several years. Micron faces a similar situation, with much of its planned capital expenditure focused on new facilities rather than immediately increasing output.

On the demand side, Zourmpanos believes Nvidia recently offered an important confirmation that AI infrastructure spending remains strong. Nvidia’s outlook points to continued rapid growth, suggesting demand for the memory required by AI systems could remain robust. Micron is also investing in next-generation memory, packaging and computing technologies, potentially giving it opportunities beyond the current HBM cycle.

The stock might have pulled back recently, but is still up by 688% over the past year. yet despite the huge gains, the 5-star investor believes its valuation remains surprisingly low because earnings expectations have increased faster than the stock price. Micron trades at roughly 6.2 times projected FY2027 earnings, based on consensus EPS of around $155. The market appears to be assuming those profits represent a cyclical peak, with earnings expected to decline significantly from FY2029 onwards.

That makes the biggest risk relatively clear. If new capacity from Micron, SK hynix and Samsung arrives around 2028 while AI demand simultaneously weakens, memory prices and margins could fall sharply. For Zourmpanos, however, the evidence currently suggests the shortage could persist much longer than investors expect.

All told, these developments have strengthened Zourmpanos’ outlook on Micron. SK hynix’s warning that memory shortages could persist through 2030 suggests meaningful supply relief remains years away, while Nvidia’s outlook indicates that demand for AI infrastructure is still running strong. The investor believes the market may therefore be underestimating how long Micron’s earnings power can last. The company’s September 30 earnings report should provide an important test of whether that thesis is beginning to play out.

To this end, Zourmpanos rates the stock a Strong Buy. (To watch Zourmpanos’ track record, click here)

BofA analyst Tal Liani covers both names and after assessing the pair’s prospects, comes down heavily in favor of one over the other.

Looking at Microsoft, Liani believes its F4Q26 results provided “further validation of its AI strategy.” Azure growth accelerated from 39% in Q3 to 43% in Q4, while management guided for growth of 45% in 1Q27. Paid M365 Copilot seats surpassed 30 million, with net additions more than doubling sequentially, while RPO rose 84% year-over-year.

The analyst also points to Microsoft’s strategy of maintaining a wide selection of internally developed and third-party AI models. This allows customers to select an appropriate model based on the requirements and economics of each workload, while Microsoft retains control over how users operate within the system. Since many tasks do not require the capabilities of an expensive frontier model, Liani believes this flexibility can improve efficiency and limit token consumption.

Microsoft is also working to extract more value from its AI infrastructure. Liani highlights three areas of focus, including improvements to engineering and software throughout the company’s CPU and GPU fleet. These efforts have helped increase the throughput of Copilot workloads fourfold so far this year. At the same time, Microsoft has almost halved the time needed to put new GPUs into operation across its largest regions, allowing additional capacity to be monetized more quickly.

“We remain constructive on the company’s long-term positioning across AI infrastructure, models and applications,” Liani said.

Accordingly, Liani rates MSFT stock a Buy and, reflecting “accelerating cloud growth and improved visibility into investment returns,” he has also raised his price objective from $500 to $600, implying shares will gain 19% over the coming year.

Salesforce receives a far less enthusiastic assessment. The company is coming off a much better-than-expected quarter, with investors subsequently sending shares up by almost 23% in the aftermath.

For Liani, however, the significance of the results goes beyond the headline numbers. He argues that the quarter was encouraging because it undermined the argument that AI will ultimately make Salesforce obsolete. Instead, the focus of the debate is moving away from whether AI will replace CRM platforms and toward whether Salesforce can successfully turn AI adoption into additional revenue growth. The latest results suggest that the underlying CRM business remains steady while the company’s AI initiatives “continue to gain traction.”

AI still accounts for only a modest portion of Salesforce’s business. Agentforce ARR stands at $1.5 billion compared with a $46 billion revenue base. Nevertheless, Liani acknowledges that Salesforce is making tangible progress in incorporating AI into its platform and generating revenue from it. Agentforce ARR has risen by more than 240% YoY, platform usage continues to expand, and the partnership with Anthropic adds an “important context across additional surfaces.” Another encouraging sign is that around half of Agentforce bookings came from credit refills, pointing to continued customer use and recurring engagement.

However, that is not enough to alter Liani’s bearish thesis.

Liani reiterated an Underperform (i.e., Sell) rating on an “unbalanced risk/reward setup with moderate growth levels, AI being too nascent to impact the revenue profile, and current valuation at the high-end of peers.”

Liani’s $160 price objective remains the Street’s lowest and suggests the stock is overvalued by 38%. (To watch Liani’s track record, click here)
